summary: Mission Health Command Center is a decision-support dashboard that helps flight surgeons see when an astronaut’s blood and immune biomarkers drift from that astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline, and explains why. It is built entirely on real NASA data: 196 measurements from the Inspiration4 mission in NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569 and OSD-575), covering 4 anonymized subjects, 7 timepoints (92 days before launch to 194 days after landing) and 7 biomarkers (white blood cells, lymphocytes, hemoglobin, platelets, glucose, sodium, interleukin-6). A rule-based engine raises “watch” or “flagged” signals and gives a plain-language reason for each. A Recovery Trajectory view shows when each biomarker returned to within 20% of baseline. It addresses the challenge by turning open NASA data into transparent, explainable monitoring. It is decision support, not diagnosis.
details:
What it does: The app compares every post-flight measurement with the same astronaut’s own pre-flight average. It flags large deviations with an explanation. Lab reference ranges are shown where they exist; interleukin-6 has none, so it is judged against baseline only. Example: subject C001’s IL-6 is 6.86 pg/mL at the first draw after landing, versus a 3.80 baseline (+80.7%).

Data and rigor: All values are parsed from NASA’s published CSV files with a Python ETL script; nothing is simulated. Subjects stay anonymized (C001–C004) as NASA published them. We found one clinically implausible platelet value in NASA’s file (C003, L-92 = 12.9, lab range 140–400). We kept it visible with a caveat and excluded it from that subject’s baseline. The Recovery Trajectory view is computed only from measured timepoints, with no extrapolation. A separate panel cites published research on risk in longer missions and is clearly walled off from our data.

Findings (4 subjects only, descriptive): hemoglobin and sodium were back within 20% of baseline at the first post-flight draw for all four subjects. IL-6 and absolute lymphocytes were slowest: only 2 of 4 subjects met the criterion by day 194.

Tools: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Framer Motion, Python.

Limits: 4 subjects, one 3-day mission, discrete timepoints only. No live vitals stream is publicly available.

SI use: code, data-processing scripts and documentation were developed with AI assistance (Claude) and reviewed by the developer. The demo narration voice is AI-generated (Kokoro TTS). No AI-generated imagery; no NASA branding used.
